https://telex.hu/transtelex/2026/08/14/l.text: Menü Kereső A román katonai radarok nem látták, lezuhant és felrobbant egy drón a Duna-deltában Transtelex Vig Emese (Transtelex) Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Újabb drón zuhant le Románia területén : a Duna-delta térségében földet érő repülő szerkezet becsapódáskor felrobbant, majd kigyulladt. Mindezt úgy, hogy a román hadsereg felügyeleti radarjai észre sem vették a határsértő szerkezet közeledtét. Egy nappal korábban, csütörtökön valóságos orosz dróninvázió volt Tulcea megyében, három drón hatolt be a romániai területre, és miattuk levegőbe is emelkedtek a vadászgépek. Ezúttal azonban úgy hatolt be a román légtérbe a drón, hogy még csak nem is érzékelték a jelenlétét. A pénteki becsapódás a Luncavița település közelében, egy fás-erdős részen történt, alig öt kilométerre az ukrán határtól. A helyi katasztrófavédelemhez a segélyhívón érkezett a bejelentés, miszerint egy alacsonyan szálló drón zuhant a fák közé, a becsapódást pedig detonáció követte, ami azonnal lángra lobbantotta a környező aljnövényzetet. A helyszínre tűzoltókat riasztottak egy rohamkocsival. A lángok a gyors beavatkozásnak köszönhetően elültek, a pontos roncsmező felkutatására pedig külön csapatokat szerveztek. A tűzoltók mellett helyi erdészek fésülik át a nehezen járható területet, a védelmi minisztérium vizsgálóbizottsága pedig egy katonai helikopterrel szállt ki a helyszínre. A védelmi tárca kénytelen volt elismerni: a légtérellenőrző rendszerek képernyőjén a drónnak nyoma sem volt, mert a szerkezet rendkívül alacsonyan repült, így észrevétlenül juthatott el a becsapódási pontig. Bár a Nemzeti Katonai Parancsnokság jelzésére 11:45-kor RO-Alert riasztást adtak ki Észak-Tulcea és Kelet-Galați lakosságának az esetlegesen lezuhanó tárgyak veszélye miatt, magáról a közvetlen behatolásról a hatóságok megint csak a lakossági 112-es hívásokból értesültek, utólag. A pénteki eset a csütörtöki, felfokozott légiriadók közvetlen folytatása. Egy nappal korábban a román légvédelem még észlelte az ukrán határ mentén mozgó orosz drónrajokat, felküldték a román F–16-os és szövetséges F–18-as vadászgépeket, a határt rövid időre átlépő célpontokat pedig nyomon tudták követni. A pénteki detonáció azonban azt bizonyítja, hogy a radarkép alatti holttérben érkező szerkezetekre nincs válasz, és ezek biztonsági kockázatot jelentenek a határ menti térségben. Egy júniusi összesítés szerint az ukrajnai háború kitörése óta az orosz drónok legalább 28 alkalommal sértették meg Románia légterét, és körülbelül 47 esetben találtak drónmaradványokat az ország területén. 2025 februárjában fogadta el a román parlament azt a törvényt, amely lehetővé teszi, hogy a hadsereg fellépjen az ország légterébe engedély nélkül belépő drónokkal és más légi járművekkel szemben. Ennek ellenére 2026. május végén nem tudták lelőni azt az orosz drónt, amely az eddigi legsúlyosabb incidenst okozta. A 30 kg robbanóanyagot szállító orosz Geran–2 típusú drón akkor közvetlenül egy tízemeletes lakóházba csapódott Galac városában. Végül 2026. július 24-én Buzău megyében lőtték le az első drónt. Ez Bukaresttől alig 90 kilométerre van, vagyis az incidens jóval közelebb történt a fővároshoz, mint a korábbi esetek és a most történt drónos robbanás – ezek helyszínei a határ menti megyék települései voltak. https://www.politico.eu/article/meet-the.text: August Hanning spent seven years at the top of Germany’s foreign intelligence service, the BND, with access to some of the country’s most closely guarded secrets. Then came a second act: private consulting, corporate intelligence and business stretching across Europe, into Russia and Asia. Now, the 80-year-old former spymaster is himself at the center of an espionage investigation, after German federal prosecutors arrested him Tuesday on suspicion of treasonous espionage, attempted treason and other espionage offenses. They allege he obtained a stream of secret intelligence from his former chief of staff and used the material to benefit his private consulting business. “It’s catastrophic for Germany and for Western intelligence services. Everyone is in shock. The scale of it is enormous, especially at a moment like this,” said one EU intelligence official, who — like others in this report — was granted anonymity to discuss a clandestine arena. “And given that investigators stumbled across this while working on an entirely separate case, we’re likely to learn much more.” Advertisement For the BND, the case comes at an uncomfortable moment. Just last week, German parliamentarians began debating a new law proposed by Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government to grant the agency sweeping new authority, as part of an effort to return Berlin’s foreign intelligence service to the top ranks of global espionage. The timing is equally awkward for European intelligence more broadly. With Russian hybrid attacks continuously targeting Europe, governments across the bloc are rewriting decades-old security laws to give their spy agencies greater powers and be taken more seriously. Prosecutors say Hanning’s former chief of staff, identified under German privacy rules as Manfred D., supplied him with roughly 2,000 BND documents between 2010 and June 2022. Many contained classified information intended exclusively for internal intelligence work, including material used to brief senior German officials. In comments to German newspaper WELT, a lawyer representing Hanning said some of the allegations against the ex-spymaster were true but that he did not harm Germany. “He was in possession of confidential documents. Incorrect, however, is the accusation that he had passed on information contained therein to the detriment of the Federal Republic of Germany — let alone [for] payment. Further investigations will show that,” he said. In one case, prosecutors suspect Hanning used classified material to prepare an analysis for an employee of foreign intelligence service. They also allege he maintained a relationship with a representative of another foreign intelligence service for several years, passing along political information that was partly based on material obtained from Manfred D. Prosecutors have not publicly identified either foreign service but German media has named Azerbaijan and Kazakhstan . Azerbaijan has denied any connection. Advertisement “In intelligence services, everything is logged — who accesses which documents and when. If an analyst working on right-wing extremism suddenly started looking at intelligence on China, that would raise red flags. But the position of chief of staff has access to virtually everything, so it wouldn’t look suspicious because of the seniority of the position,” said a second EU intelligence official. Chiefs of staff often stay on when directors change, unless they don’t get along with the incoming boss, the official added. “Every intelligence service will now be looking at what information it shared with the BND and assessing what damage may have been done,” he said. Revolving door Hanning led the BND from 1998 to 2005, before serving as state secretary at Germany’s interior ministry until 2009. Once out of government, he wasted little time entering the private sector. In July 2010, Hanning and his wife established Hanning Consult. It was in the spring of that same year that Manfred D. agreed to provide him with intelligence from inside the BND in exchange for payment, according to the prosecutor’s statement. Hanning then used that information in his private consulting activities, they added. Roderich Kiesewetter, a Christian Democrat lawmaker on the Foreign Affairs Committee in the German parliament, said that within Germany there is a “very widespread network” of people who use the contacts and knowledge acquired while they were in service to influence Berlin’s policy on behalf of foreign governments like Russia and China. Advertisement “It’s not only sad, it’s damaging the reputation of Germany,” Kiesewetter told POLITICO. “You could also say if you want to talk to Russia, take former members of the government or former members of the secret services.” Hanning also became involved with Samuel Danilowitsch, a German businessman, who led the Swiss corporate intelligence consultancy, Pluteos. There, Hanning eventually became chairman and the two were listed as attending a 2019 Moscow gathering focused on Europe-Russia relations, attended by Russian political and business figures, where the annexation of Crimea was brought up as a “necessity” rather than a choice. Pluteos did not respond to a request for comment. From around 2014, Hanning joined British consultancy G3 as a senior adviser, according to archived web pages seen by POLITICO. He later oversaw its work involving Russia and the former Soviet republics, according to German media outlet Correctiv. G3 did not respond to a request for comment. In 2019, Hanning was invited as a “guest of honor” to a gathering organized by Russia’s Security Council of officials and experts from Arctic Council countries. It was chaired by former secretary of the Security Council of Russia, Nikolai Patrushev, one of the most powerful figures in President Vladimir Putin’s security orbit. As part of the cultural program, the group visited the remote Valaam Island monastery where Hanning was pictured next to Patrushev. Delegates from Arctic Council countries visited the Valaam Island monastery on Oct. 2, 2019. August Hanning stands on the far right of the front row, next to senior Russian security official Nikolai Patrushev. | Valaam monastery Hanning has also publicly ventured into some of the more politically explosive questions surrounding Russia’s war on Ukraine. In 2024, he told WELT TV that he considered it “very likely” that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy knew about the 2022 operation that destroyed the Nord Stream pipelines. Days later, Hanning went further, suggesting an agreement between senior Ukrainian and Polish figures was behind the attack. Germany has since charged a Ukrainian national it identified only as Serhii K., with his trial due to begin in Hamburg in October. Advertisement None of those business relationships, contacts or statements establishes a connection to the espionage case now facing Hanning, though they paint a picture of the influence he continued to amass after leaving the German government. Prosecutors have not accused him of spying for Russia. The steakhouse heiress Investigators got onto Hanning’s trail starting with an extraordinary custody dispute involving Christina Block, an heiress to a German steakhouse empire. Block is accused by the Hamburg Public Prosecutor’s Office of orchestrating the abduction of her two youngest children from their father in Denmark. Prosecutors in that case say Block and two men commissioned an Israeli security team to seize her children, then aged 10 and 13, from their father, Stephan Hensel. According to the indictment, masked men beat Hensel and took the children across the Danish-German border, to southern Germany. The children were reunited with their father in Denmark four days later, under a court order. Block denies knowing about the abduction. In September 2025, Hamburg investigators searched Hanning’s home and business premises in connection with the Block case, according to local media . Prosecutors suspected Hanning and a retired police officer had accepted a contract worth more than €100,000 to intercept the children on their way to school in November 2022. The plan ultimately failed as their father noticed suspicious figures and alerted Danish police. German broadcaster Taggeschau reported that the investigators, in the search of Hanning’s premises, discovered around 2,000 digital BND documents that ultimately triggered scrutiny of his handling of sensitive government information. Federal prosecutors took over the resulting investigation in May 2026. Advertisement Manfred D. had been Hanning’s chief of staff at the intelligence service and subsequently served several of Hanning’s successors, remaining in a senior position until March this year. Both men are now in custody. “He’s reflecting the Germany between 1998 and 2011, so he has not the feeling of having done something evil,” said Kiesewetter. “He was just mirroring [the] state policy of the center-right Christian Democratic and conservative political alliance.” Hans von der Burchard contributed to this report.

https://www.aol.com/articles/rescuers-pu.text: By HANNA ARHIROVA Updated Fri, October 9, 2026 at 12:37 AM UTC 28 KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — A Russian-guided bomb exploded next to public buses filled with passengers in eastern Ukraine, authorities said Thursday, killing 30 people as part of a wave of attacks that also worsened power outages in the capital. The morning attack occurred next to a bus stop in the war-torn city of Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, prompting public transport to be suspended in the area. “There is no doubt that Russia is cynically targeting civilians,” Oleksandr Honcharenko, head of the city's military administration, said, adding that the rescue effort had been hampered by subsequent Russian attacks using small drones. Russia and Ukraine are locked in a long-range aerial war while their armies remain largely deadlocked on the front line, more than 4 1/2 years since Moscow’s full-scale invasion. Russia has escalated its aerial attack in recent weeks, putting pressure on Ukraine as it prepares for winter and hitting the infrastructure keeping its war-battered economy afloat. Recent targets have included energy systems, key industries, railways, post offices, shopping centers, telecom networks, gas stations and grain exports. Thursday's attack followed a Russian missile strike a day earlier that killed 22, including five children, in the northern Ukrainian town of Pryluky . Rescuers were searching the rubble of a residential building . At least 54 people were wounded. Several survivors slept in heavily damaged apartments because they couldn't find anywhere else to stay. Ukraine appeals for more defense support from NATO Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy traveled to Pryluky on Thursday with visiting British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who announced new sanctions on Russia. Zelenskyy warned that Russia will likely escalate daily missile and drone attacks as winter approaches. He appealed for additional defense support from NATO countries. “It is important that support in words takes concrete form in new packages for Ukraine’s defense,” he wrote in an online post. “Supplies of anti-ballistic capabilities, ammunition for our combat aircraft and investments in interceptors — all of this is directly helping save lives every day.” In audio clips responding to journalist’s questions Thursday evening, Zelenskyy said a Ukrainian delegation would meet in the U.S. with President Donald Trump’s representatives Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff for two days beginning Friday to discuss strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses, among other issues. Ukraine's energy company DTEK said national grid operator Ukrenergo had ordered emergency power outages in Kyiv. Regular, rolling outages that occur on a schedule across the country will be halted during these shutdowns. Advertisement Officials are urging families to prepare emergency kits, store drinking water and maintain backup power sources, as Moscow keeps up the intensity of its attacks. Kyiv police said bomb disposal specialists defused two unexploded ballistic missile warheads, each weighing about half a ton, after they landed near residential buildings. Late Wednesday, Russian drones struck Kyiv’s Obolonskyi and Desnianskyi districts, killing four people and injuring 12, including four children, police said. Ukrainian attacks damage data center and oil refinery Russian technology giant Yandex said one of its data centers in the western Ryazan region was damaged in a Ukrainian drone attack, taking the site offline. Also Thursday, Ukraine said its forces struck a large oil refinery complex in the city of Salavat, some 1,200 kilometers (about 750 miles) east of Moscow. Ukraine's General Staff described the complex as one of Russia’s largest oil refining and petrochemical facilities. The claim could not be independently verified. Ukrainian drones also reached Russia’s Omsk region in western Siberia, more than 2,000 kilometers (1,242 miles) from the border with Ukraine. Omsk regional Gov. Vitaly Khotsenko said most of the drones were shot down by air defenses, but one “reached a northern industrial hub.” He didn’t elaborate. Russian independent news outlet Astra reported that the Omsk oil refinery was on fire after the attack. There was no official confirmation of the report. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said his government presented proposals to both Russia and Ukraine aimed at protecting civilian shipping in the Black Sea, while warning that commercial trade and grain exports could be disrupted by escalating military offensives. Separately, Lithuania deployed about 100 additional soldiers to help secure the NATO member's border with the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad, the Baltic country's defense minister, Robertas Kaunas, said. Sandwiched between Lithuania and Poland, Kaliningrad is separated from mainland Russia and remains a major security concern for NATO’s eastern flank. ___ Associated Press writers Suzan Fraser in Ankara, Turkey; Liudas Dapkus in Vilnius, Lithuania; Derek Gatopoulos in Athens, Greece and Jamey Keaten in Geneva contributed. ___ Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine Show comments 28 Advertisement From Our Partners Advertisement Entertainment Entertainment Entertainment Weekly Wynonna Judd says mother Naomi foreshadowed her suicide: 'She talked about it a lot' Entertainment USA TODAY Miss Universe whistleblower speaks out after alleged extortion Finance Finance Reuters Ozempic wave boosts US cobblers and tailors as Americans tighten their belts Finance Reuters IMF, OECD warn AI could widen rich-poor country divide Food Food Health We Asked 3 Dietitians To Name the Healthiest Nut—They All Picked the Same One Food Bored Panda 43 fun and simple food hacks that even the most inexperienced may find useful Lighter Side Lighter Side Worcester Telegram Move over, candy: Potatoes are Halloween's hottest new treat Lighter Side USA TODAY What scares Stephen King?
